reasons: Passages read as claimed: HyAphr 6 and Il. 16.670/680, Od. 24.59, 7.265 have the stock Greek line with ἄμβροτα + εἵματα + a form of ἕννυμι; RV 6.75.18b (= AVŚ 7.118.1) has amŕ̥tena with the imperative vastām of vas- 'wear, clothe' (the automatic mapping to h₂wes- 'dwell' is wrong; the claim's reading is right); AVŚ 9.1.2 has amṛtam with the participle vasānāṃ. Etymology exact: amŕ̥ta- = ἄμβροτος (*n̥-mr̥-tó-), vas- = ἕννυμι/εἷμα (*wes-). The relation is congruent at the level 'clothe (a body) in/with the immortal': Greek puts the adjective on the garment noun, Vedic uses the substantivised neuter as the covering, and Greek has the substantive ἀμβροσίῃ beside it in Il. 16.670/680, so the drift is defensible. Context is close: a body made inviolable or divine by what it is dressed or anointed with (Sarpedon's corpse; the warrior's armour charm). Not derivative. Caveats: the Vedic side is a single collocation (RV has amŕ̥ta- + vas- 2 together only here and 2.10.1c), and ἄμβροτος is a very common epithet, hence medium generic risk.

Anchors are present (Hippocratic prose lines confirmed by string search in De flatibus, Aphorismi, De humoribus; AVŚ 13.1.s96; AVŚ 7.18.s3; Od. 7.118). Only the 'winter' member is cognate (χειμών ~ hima-, *ǵʰeym-); the hot member is θέρος in Greek but ghraṃsa- in the Vedic anchor, a different derivative. The Hippocratic anchors are technical season lists, not phraseology. A winter/summer merism for 'the whole year' is what any language forms, and the negated pair of Od. 7.118 ('neither in winter nor summer') does not match the Vedic negated clauses (heat did not burn, cold did not strike) in relation. Generic.

reasons: Passages checked: RV 1.105.11c (the eagles keep the wolf off the paths, next pada: as he crosses the waters), RV 1.105.18b (the wolf saw me going on the path), TOROT spi 159 (Vseslav, as a wolf, crossed the path of Khors). Cognates are sound (vŕ̥ka- ~ вълкъ, pánthā- ~ путь). But the relations differ: in the Vedic, ablative 'from the paths' with the wolf as object of 'keep away'; in the Old Russian, instrumental 'as a wolf' (manner, a shape-shifter) with 'path' as object of 'run across'. The 'path' in RV 1.105 is not shown to be a sun path. Wolf + path is a frequent, generic pairing, the verbs are unrelated, and the Slovo is a single late (and authenticity-debated) text. Coincidence.

Anchors read as claimed: Od. 20.69 (μέλιτι + γλυκερῷ in a list of foods), Lucr. 1.938 and 1.947 (= 4.13, 4.22, the honey-rimmed cup), Plaut. Asin. 614 (comparative to a lover); support Il. 1.249, 18.109 checked. The Greek–Latin cognates are real but only two-branch: μέλι = mel (*mélit) and γλυκύς = dulcis; de Vaan (s.v. dulcis) notes the Graeco-Latin *dl(u)ku- has no further cognates and may be a shared borrowing. In each language these are simply the ordinary words for 'honey' and 'sweet', so their co-occurrence is predicted by the lexicon, and honey as the measure of sweetness ('sweeter than honey') is near-universal. Independence is also weak: Lucretius' honey-rimmed cup image and Plautus' comedies draw on Greek models. Generic.

Passages checked: Eur. Rhes. 816 (oath, Ζεὺς and πατήρ separated by the verb), AVŚ 6.120.s4 (dyaur + pitā, with bhūmir + mātā in the preceding verse), Cato Agr. 132.2 and 134.3 (vocative Iupiter in sacrificial prayer, alongside the vocative of Janus with pater). Exact cognates in all three branches: Ζεύς = dyáuḥ = Iu- (*dyḗws), πατήρ = pitā́ = -piter (*ph₂tḗr), in apposition naming the sky-god; Latin has univerbated the vocative into the theonym. Same referent, same title, same prayer/oath register; not generic (no generic reason for the sky to be the god systematically called 'father' in three branches) and not derivative (Cato's prayers are native Roman ritual). The Latin anchor carries the formula only in the fused name, which is itself the evidence of an old fixed phrase.

Anchors: Xen. Cyr. 2.1.29 (string confirmed) has only the noun ἱδρῶτα as object of 'provide', no figura and no toil word; RV 10.106.10c has the figura svédam + āsiṣvidānā́ (ploughmen 'having sweated sweat'). Etymology good: ἱδρώς and svéda-/svid- from *sweyd-, Beekes s.v. In support, Il. 4.27 has the same figura (ἱδρῶ + ἵδρωσα) beside toil (μόγῳ, καμέτην), and RV 1.86.8ab pairs śaśamānásya with svédasya, so sweat + *ḱemh₂- toil occurs in both. The Greek anchor does not carry it, and a cognate-object figura with 'sweat' plus sweat as the mark of labour are natural in any language, so this is defensible but not compelling.

Anchors are misaligned: RV 9.74.1c has diváḥ with rétasā 'seed', not a rain word; RV 10.98.10c has neither word (diváḥ + vr̥ṣṭím are in 10.98.10d); only Il. 11.493 has Διὸς + ὄμβρῳ. The RV count holds (18 padas with div- + vr̥ṣṭí-), but many are plainly ablative 'rain from heaven' (with pári, várṣanti, 'flow'), so the Vedic phrase is not a genitive of the god matching Διός. Only one element is cognate (diváḥ/Διός); the head noun differs (vr̥ṣṭí- vs ὄμβρος, whose cognate abhrá- means 'cloud'). 'Rain from/of the sky' is what any language says. Generic.

Passages read as claimed: Lucr. 1.271, 6.592, 5.1226 (uis + uenti as agent of violent motion at sea/in the earth); Il. 15.383, Od. 9.71, 13.276, 19.186, Il. 17.739, Hes. Op. 518 (ἲς + ἀνέμοιο/ἀνέμου, line-end formula). Only the head noun is cognate: uīs = ἴς (*wiH-s, de Vaan s.v. vis); the dependent is renewed (uentus vs ἄνεμος). In Latin uis + genitive is the ordinary way to say 'force of X'; of the 16 LASLA units with uis + uentus, 13 are in Lucretius book 6 (Epicurean meteorology from Greek sources) and the rest elsewhere in Lucretius, a poet who imitates Homer, so the Latin is not independent. 'The force of the wind' is a generic phrase; the Greek fossil ἴς is interesting but a one-sided archaism does not make a shared phrase.

Passages: Lucr. 5.692 (the sun 'creeping' through the zodiac, closing the seasons); AVŚ 4.20.s17 (do not hide the piśāca, 'creeping like the sun in the clear sky'), where sarpantam may as well agree with piśācam as with sūryam. Etymology fine (sōl ~ sūrya-, serpens = sárpant-). But each side is a single occurrence (no other sun + sr̥p- collocation in AV, none in RV in this corpus), *serp- is the ordinary verb for slow gliding motion in both languages, and the contexts (astronomy vs a demon-seeing charm simile) are not congruent. Nothing beyond the lexicon predicts the match. Coincidence.

Passages: Arist. EN 5.1129a (string: the key with which doors are locked, a homonymy example), Od. 19.30 (κλήϊσεν + θύρας), Lucr. 4.598 (clausis + foribus), Plaut. Asin. 759 (fores + occlusae). θύρα = fores (*dʰwer-, de Vaan s.v. foris) is exact; κλῄω and claudo share only the root *kleh₂w- 'peg' and are separate formations (de Vaan: claudo < *kleh₂u-d- or a derivative of clavis/clavus). 'Shut the door(s)' with the language's ordinary words is not phraseology; the Aristotle anchor is philosophical prose. Generic.

reasons: Passages: Ar. Lys. 629 (proverbial: as trustworthy as a gaping wolf); Hyndluljóð 27 (a genealogical list of men's bynames; Ulfr + gínandi is a personal name with epithet). λύκος = ulfr is exact, but χάσκω/κέχηνα (*ǵʰh₂-) and ON gína (*ǵʰiH-n-) are at best root-related, different formations, so the second element is not a cognate pair. The contexts (proverb vs name in a list) are not congruent and a gaping wolf is an obvious image. Coincidence.

Passages: RV 1.92.5d (Dawn as diváḥ + duhitā́), Il. 4.515 (Athena) and Il. 3.374 (Aphrodite) with Διὸς + θυγάτηρ. Exact cognates: diváḥ = Διός (*diw-és/-ós), duhitár- = θυγάτηρ (*dʰugh₂tḗr), in the same relation (genitive of the sky-god + 'daughter') as a fixed honorific title of a goddess in verse, frequent on both sides (38 RV padas; many Homeric lines). The shift of referent (Dawn vs Aphrodite/Athena etc.) is a defensible drift of a title. Not generic (no language forms 'daughter of the sky' as a title by default) and not derivative.

Passages: RV 2.16.3d (Indra 'flies' with his swift ones, āśúbhiḥ + pátasi), Hes. Th. 269, h.Herm. 553, Pind. P. 1.6 (ὠκύς + πτέρυξ 'swift wings'); support compounds RV 4.26.4b āśupátvā (falcon), Il. 8.42 ὠκυπέτα (horses). ὠκύς = āśú- is exact; πτέρυξ and pat- share *pet(h₂)- but the Greek free phrase uses the noun 'wing', not the verb, so the anchors are not congruent in relation (instrumental of the steeds vs instrumental of wings). The compounds are the best evidence but differ in the second-member formation (-pátvan- vs -πέτης). 'Swift-flying' is a semantically obvious combination, and both languages compound ὠκυ-/āśu- freely. Defensible, not compelling.

The formula *dyēu- + *ph₂tēr is genuine (see the Vedic anchors AVŚ 3.23.s14 and 8.7.s4, dyauḥ + pitā, the plants' father Sky), but the Greek and Latin anchors do not carry it: Xen. Cyr. 1.6.1 (sentence read) has the cult epithet πατρῷος 'ancestral' on Zeus, a derivative adjective used also of Hestia in the same clause, not apposed 'father'; Cato Agr. 141.2 has Iouem (oblique of Iuppiter, without -piter) with pater given to Mars. Graded on anchor quality: one branch carries the phrase, the others only drifted or split pieces.

Passages: Plaut. Asin. 614 and Lucr. 1.947 as in the other honey claims; Pind. P. 6.50 has γλυκεῖα qualifying φρήν and μελισσᾶν 'of bees' in a different clause (not a sweet-honey collocation); Simonides 7.510.3 has γλυκεροῦ qualifying νόστου with the compound μελίφρονος (not 'honey'). So two of four anchors are misread. The Greek–Latin cognates are real but only two-branch: μέλι = mel (*mélit) and γλυκύς = dulcis; de Vaan (s.v. dulcis) notes the Graeco-Latin *dl(u)ku- has no further cognates and may be a shared borrowing. In each language these are simply the ordinary words for 'honey' and 'sweet', so their co-occurrence is predicted by the lexicon, and honey as the measure of sweetness ('sweeter than honey') is near-universal. Independence is also weak: Lucretius' honey-rimmed cup image and Plautus' comedies draw on Greek models. Generic.

Passages: AVŚ 3.23.s14 and 8.7.s4 (plants 'whose father is Sky, mother Earth'), AVŚ 12.1.s26 (Earth mother, Parjanya father), and [Arist.] De plantis 1.2.817a (sentence read: Anaxagoras said earth is mother of plants, the sun father). The Greek De plantis is a medieval retroversion, so its wording is not ancient Greek phraseology (derivative). In the Greek only the kin terms are cognate (μήτηρ = mātā́, πατήρ = pitā́); both cosmic nouns are renewed (γῆ, ἥλιος), so the claimed phrase is absent; and assigning earth/sky (or sun) as mother/father of growing things is cross-culturally common. The real inherited piece, *dyēus ph₂tēr, is not in the Greek anchor.

'The force of the wind' is a generic phrase; the Greek fossil ἴς is interesting but a one-sided archaism does not make a shared phrase.

Anchors: Cato Agr. 141.3 (the full LASLA unit has pecua and salua with seruassis, beside pastores, in Mars' lustration prayer, before the address to Mars as pater); AVŚ 12.2.s29 (horses, men=vīreṣu, cows, goats, sheep), AVŚ 11.2.s45 (cows, men=puruṣeṣu), AVŚ 11.2.s18 (puruṣa among the five paśavaḥ). The anchors carry the merism only partly (Latin renews 'men' with pastores; the AV lines use vīra + go, or paśu + puruṣa). The exact pair is in support and checked: Umbrian Iguvine prayer (Buck 1904, ueiro + pequo with salua + seritu, which matches the Latin salua + seruassis), Avestan CAB YtFra2.10 (protection of pasuuā̊ + vīraiiā̊), YtZam8.3 (pasu + vīra 'undying'), AVP 19.56 (paśubhiś + vīraiḥ, refrain), AVŚ 11.1. Cognates exact: *peḱu- (pecu, paśu-, pasu-, pequo) and *wiHro- (vīra-, ueiro). Same speech act in three branches: a prayer that men and cattle be kept safe. A men-and-cattle merism is natural for herders, but the identical lexical pair in a fixed protective-prayer frame across Italic and Indo-Iranian goes beyond that. Accepted on the support; the anchors alone would be weak.

Passages: Plaut. Asin. 614, Lucr. 1.947, and Xenophanes fr. 34 (= 38 DK: if god had not made honey, men would say figs were far sweeter, γλύσσονα in the next line). The Xenophanes is a genuine honey-as-standard comparative, but it remains the same universal image with the ordinary words. The Greek–Latin cognates are real but only two-branch: μέλι = mel (*mélit) and γλυκύς = dulcis; de Vaan (s.v. dulcis) notes the Graeco-Latin *dl(u)ku- has no further cognates and may be a shared borrowing. In each language these are simply the ordinary words for 'honey' and 'sweet', so their co-occurrence is predicted by the lexicon, and honey as the measure of sweetness ('sweeter than honey') is near-universal. Independence is also weak: Lucretius' honey-rimmed cup image and Plautus' comedies draw on Greek models. Generic.

Passages: Demades fr. 42 (string confirmed: man yoked the ox to the plough), Cato Agr. 138.1 (oxen may be yoked on holidays), Agr. 10.2 (inventory: ploughs, yokes, ox harness), Cato Orig. fr. 11 (three oxen to one plough), AVP 19.51.s26 (luck to the yoked draught animal). Cognates are sound (*yewg-, *gʷṓws, *h₂érh₃trom), but this is the technical vocabulary of an inherited technology: once 'yoke', 'ox' and 'plough' are inherited, 'yoke the ox to the plough' follows necessarily. Inventories and late prose are not phraseology. Generic.

Passages: Il. 23.294, 16.148, 24.14 (ὠκέας + ἵππους as object of yoking, ζυγόν/ζεύξειεν); RV 1.118.4b and 1.140.4d (the swift ones, āśávaḥ, yoked to the chariot), AVP 19.34.s24 (race charm, āśīyān + aśva). Support checked: RV 1.117.9b = 7.71.5b āśúm + áśvam; Avestan CAB has the compound āsu.aspa- 'having swift horses' (3 times). Exact cognates: ὠκύς = āśú- = āsu-, ἵππος = áśva- = aspa-, with *yewg- (ζεύγνυμι/ζυγόν = yuj-) in the yoking context on both sides. The adjective is one of several possible words for 'fast' in each language, and the noun-epithet pair is fixed (35 Homeric lines, several RV padas, a lexicalised Avestan compound). 'Swift horses' is semantically natural (medium generic risk), but the same epithet root in a fixed pairing and a compound in three branches is not chance.

Passages: Solon fr. 36 quoted in Ath. Pol. 12.4 (sentence read: verse, Earth as μήτηρ + μεγίστη of the Olympian gods, witness in the court of Time); AVŚ 7.6.s7 (Aditi as mātaraṃ + mahīm); RV 1.72.9d (mātā́ Aditi with sons); RV 1.164.33b and AVŚ 9.10.s23 (mātā́ + pr̥thivī́ + mahī́); AVŚ 12.1.s26; AVŚ 3.23.s14. Cognates exact (*méh₂tēr, *meǵh₂-), in the same attributive relation, for the same referent, in invocations. Against it: 'great mother' of Earth or a mother goddess is close to universal, the Earth noun is renewed on both sides, Greek has a superlative, and the Vedic 'great mother' of 7.6 is Aditi, equated with Earth only by inference. I weigh universality heavily here: defensible but not compelling.

reasons: Passages: AVŚ 4.27.s3 (utsam + akṣitaṃ, the Maruts' never-failing spring); h.Ven. 43 (Greek anchor has only ἄφθιτα qualifying μήδεα, not water, so it is misaligned). The one Greek water collocation is Hes. Th. 805 (Styx's ἄφθιτον + ὕδωρ), checked. ákṣita- = ἄφθιτος is exact, but útsa- (*ud-s-o-) and ὕδωρ (*wód-r̥) are different derivatives of the water root, so the noun is root-cognate only, and both adjectives combine freely with many nouns. Context differs (a spring that is milked vs the primeval water of the gods' oath). A single Greek attestation; defensible but weak.

Passages: RV 8.62.5a-b (Indra makes bold the mánaḥ even of the bold, dhr̥ṣát); Il. 16.242 (Zeus asked to embolden, θάρσυνον, the ἦτορ). The Greek anchor renews the inner-seat noun (ἦτορ), so only *dʰers- is cognate there; support Il. 5.2 and Od. 1.321 have μένος + θάρσος but coordinated as two objects of 'give/put', not 'bold mind'. Etymology good (dhr̥ṣ- ~ θαρσ-, mánas- = μένος). A god giving courage to a man's heart is common idiom; relation and verbs differ. One element per anchor pair; weak.

reasons: Passages: RV 9.86.44c (Soma leaves his husk 'as a snake' creeps out of its jūrṇā́m + tvácam 'aged skin'); Arist. HA 5.17 (string confirmed: crustaceans shed their shell as snakes the 'so-called' γῆρας); PA 4.13 (snakes swim as they creep, ἕρπουσιν, unrelated to moulting). Cognates good: áhi- = ὄφις (*h₁ógʷʰi-), jūrṇá- and γῆρας both *ǵerh₂- (Beekes s.v. γῆρας). Both are moulting similes. But the formations differ (adjective on 'skin' vs the noun 'old age' as name of the slough), the Greek is a popular name reported in technical prose, and calling a cast skin 'old' is a natural metaphor (Latin senecta does the same with another root, which argues for independent creation). Weak.

reasons: Passages: AVŚ 3.12.s11 (the house-goddess addressed as patni and devī), Od. 1.14 (Calypso called πότνι(α) and δῖα in one line), Hes. fr. 150.31 (Calypso as πότνια nymph), AVP 19.1.s17 (devīr ... patnīḥ). patnī = πότνια (*pótnih₂, Beekes s.v.) is exact and its use as a divine title is real. The second element is not: δῖος (*diw-yo-) and devī́ (*deyw-ih₂) are different formations, and in Od. 1.14 the two words belong to two independent stock formulas that merely share a line; Greek pairs them only twice. The automatic śaraṇa ~ Καλυψώ match is spurious. One element only; weak.

Passages: h.Ven. 29 (πατὴρ + Ζεύς), h.Ap. 307 (Διὶ + πατρί), AVŚ 6.120.s4 (dyaur + pitā), AVŚ 2.28.s7 and 9.10.s23 (dyauṣ/dyaur + pitā paired with pṛthivī + mātā), Cato Agr. 132.2 (vocative Iupiter in the daps prayer). Exact cognates in three branches (*dyḗws, *ph₂tḗr), same apposition naming the sky-god as father, Latin fused into the theonym; same religious register. Not generic, not derivative. Same evidence and grade as the other Father-Sky claim whose anchors carry the formula.

Passages: AVŚ 10.4.s35 (snake charm: Indra slew, jaghāna, your first begetter, O snake, ahe); Hdt. 6.77.2 (sentence read: hexameter Delphic oracle, the dread thrice-coiled ὄφις perished, subdued by the spear). Only the serpent noun is cognate (áhi- = ὄφις). The Greek verb is renewed and passive (ἀπώλετο, δαμασθείς), and no checked Greek locus combines *gʷʰen- with ὄφις (the support has κτείνω with ὄφις, or πέφνε with δράκων). The oracle's serpent is a figure for a defeated people, not a monster slain by a god, so the context is only loosely comparable. One element in verse retellings of a famous killing; weak.

Passages: RV 1.113.13d (Dawn ajárā + amŕ̥tā); Il. 24.460 (Hermes: θεὸς + ἄμβροτος). The Greek anchor carries only the 'immortal' word, not the doublet. In Homer the doublet is ἀγήρως + ἀθάνατος (9 lines) with the non-cognate ἀθάνατος, and ἀγήρως never pairs with ἄμβροτος in the Homer or GLAUx corpora. ἀγήρως and a-jára- are privatives of the same root but not the same stem (Greek built on the s-stem γῆρας). In Vedic the pair is rare (RV 1.113.13, 3.23.1; AVŚ 10.8). 'Ageless and deathless' for gods is a natural pairing. The parallel is suggestive, but there is no exact cognate pair in the same collocation; weak.

Greek anchors carry the phrase: Hes. Sc. 373 (εὐρεῖα + χθών), and Il. 21.387 (the claim's 21.386 is the line before; 21.387 has βράχε with εὐρεῖα + χθών). The Indic anchors do not: AVŚ 11.2.s19 has pṛthivī, with uru qualifying antarikṣam (the atmosphere, not earth); RV 10.170.3d has urú + paprathe of the sun's might, not earth. The only exact Vedic match is support RV 6.17.7a (kṣā́m and urvī́m, verb-separated, possibly 'the wide one' as a separate noun); Avestan Y 10.4 has ząm with pərəϑβīm (the *pleth₂- word, not *h₁wérHu-), checked in CAB. εὐρύς = urú- and χθών = kṣám- are good. 'Wide/broad earth' is a natural epithet and the Indic evidence is thin; weak.

Passages: Hippocr. Vect. 42 and 23, De arte 10 (sentences read: surgical/anatomical lists of bones, sinews, joints), Lucr. 3.697 and 3.567 (sinews + bones), AVŚ 2.33.s11 and AVP 4.7.s9 (ablative lists of tissues in disease charms). Cognates good (ὀστέον = os = ásthi-, νεῦρον = neruus = snā́van-, de Vaan s.v. nervus). But listing a body's bones and sinews with the ordinary inherited words is what any anatomy or healing text does; the 'joints' member is only root-cognate, Vedic lacks it, and Lucretius' physiology follows Greek sources. Generic.

reasons: Passages: Ar. Thesm. 1192 (the Scythian's broken Greek: his tongue sweet like Attic honey), Plaut. Asin. 614, Lucr. 1.947 and 1.938. The speech link (Il. 1.249 and Thesm. 1192) is natural and found in many languages. The Greek–Latin cognates are real but only two-branch: μέλι = mel (*mélit) and γλυκύς = dulcis; de Vaan (s.v. dulcis) notes the Graeco-Latin *dl(u)ku- has no further cognates and may be a shared borrowing. In each language these are simply the ordinary words for 'honey' and 'sweet', so their co-occurrence is predicted by the lexicon, and honey as the measure of sweetness ('sweeter than honey') is near-universal. Independence is also weak: Lucretius' honey-rimmed cup image and Plautus' comedies draw on Greek models. Generic.

Passages: RV 1.103.4d (Indra, the son, took a name for fame; cognate words sūnúḥ, nā́ma, śrávase); Plato Leg. 9.878a (sentence read: kinsmen adopt a son into an extinct line and name him begetter and hearth-holder 'for good omen', φήμης). Only υἱός = sūnú- is exact; ὄνομα appears only inside the verb ἐπονομάζω; the 'fame' noun and the verb are renewed (φήμη here means auspicious utterance, not renown). The contexts (a god's heroic epithet vs legal adoption naming) are not congruent. Coincidence.

Passages: RV 1.124.11b (Dawn yokes, yuṅkté, the array of red cows, gávām); Hes. Op. 578-581 (Dawn sets men on the road and puts yokes, ζυγά, on oxen, βουσί). Cognates good (yuj- ~ ζυγόν, *yewg-; gáv- = βοῦς). Dawn as the subject of an act of yoking cattle in both is notable, but the relation differs: Vedic Dawn yokes her own mythic team, while Hesiod's Dawn is the time at which farmers yoke their oxen, an obvious piece of agricultural realia. The Greek uses a noun phrase with τίθημι, not the verb. Weak.

Passages: AVŚ 8.6.s48 (demons who eat raw flesh: āmaṃ + māṃsam + adanti, with kraviḥ in the parallel colon); Hippocr. De prisca medicina 13 (sentence read: boiled instead of raw meat, ὠμῶν + κρεῶν, as the step from a crude diet). Support checked: RV 1.162.10b āmásya + kravíṣaḥ; Il. 22.347 (Achilles: raw meat, κρέα, to eat, ἔδμεναι); AVŚ 11.10.s18 (raw-eating vultures on a corpse). Exact cognates: āmá- = ὠμός, kravís- = κρέας, ad- = ἔδω; and the dedicated compound ὠμηστής = āmā́d- 'raw-eater' (Beekes s.v. ὠμός notes the Skt. match), used on both sides of beasts or demons feeding on the dead. The pairing with the same value (raw flesh as the food of the savage and demonic, set against cooked) recurs in both. 'Raw meat' alone would be generic, but the matching compound and context go beyond that.
